To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
outdoor leaders believe that co‐leaders need to be good with people, good with the wilderness, and good at everything.

(1) outdoor leaders perceive co‐leaders to be more important to the success of the trip than the leader; (2) outdoor leaders perceive that co‐leadership is more important on trips of extended length than on trips of shorter length; (3) outdoor leaders perceive the most important co‐leader traits and skills to be: interpersonal skills, communication skills, and technical skills; (4) outdoor leaders perceive interpersonal skills, communication and technical skills to be more important than leadership skills; and

In summary, our research is concerned with
the co‐leadership of extended trips in the outdoors.
understanding leadership and co‐leadership dynamics on extended outdoor trips.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
leaders and co‐leaders are more alike in their leadership beliefs than they are different.
the co‐leadership skills and traits of an outdoor leader are dependent upon the leader's philosophy of leadership.

the skills and traits that outdoor trip leaders perceived as important for their co‑leaders to possess on extended outdoor trips were those that empowered their co‑leaders and allowed for the delegation of responsibility and decision making, those that allowed their co‑leaders access to power and authority, and those that allowed for the co‑leaders to be effective and efficient in their roles as co‑leaders.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
co‐leaders are important to the success of extended wilderness trips, and the skills and traits they possess are important to the trip leader.
the skills and traits that leaders perceive to be most important for a co‐leader to possess are those that are most likely to be effective in a specific leadership style and context.
co‐leadership on extended outdoor trips can be a very effective and beneficial way for leaders to work with their co‐leaders, but the co‐leader needs to be carefully chosen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the skills and traits of co‐leaders are important for outdoor leaders to consider.
outdoor leaders are not a homogenous group and that there are many leadership styles that are effective in the outdoor environment.
the leadership literature is rich with information about leadership, but there is a lack of information about the co‐leadership process in the field.
